\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:rh_intro}
% 2026-10-17 (user): prose rewritten in the style of Zhang, Zhang, Cucuringu, and Qian (2024).
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-25 (user: emphasize our lineage in the realized volatility literature): added -- the first item.
\item \textbf{Realized volatility at the intraday horizon.} Realized variance, the sum of squared high-frequency
  returns, made volatility observable and forecastable \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003,
  BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009} has become
  the benchmark for forecasting it at the daily horizon. We carry this program to a single intraday interval, the
  closing half hour of the trading day, and ask what predictors from outside the index's own price history add to

\item \textbf{Motivation for the HAR baseline.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the standard HAR regression models
  realized volatility solely as a linear function of its own past lags. Consequently, it omits a rich set of
  exogenous variables available by 15:30: higher-order realized moments of the futures; the intraday trading of
  the index's constituents, through their realized moments, liquidity, and order-flow imbalance; option-implied
  volatility; the calendar of FOMC announcements; and alternative data, namely social-media sentiment and attention
  from StockTwits and the net option vega bought by non-market-makers (volatility demand). Alternative data of this
  kind have been used to forecast daily realized volatility \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}; we
  ask whether they help at the intraday horizon.
\item \textbf{Empirical design.} For each intraday interval $(t,i)$, we consider a single forecast mapping of

\item \textbf{Realized variance and the HAR model.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the heterogeneous
  autoregressive (HAR) model specifies the conditional expectation of next-day realized variance as a linear
  function of past realized variances aggregated over daily, weekly, and monthly horizons:
  $\E_t[\RV^{(d)}_{t+1}] = \beta_0 + \beta_d\, \RV^{(d)}_t + \beta_w\, \RV^{(w)}_t + \beta_m\, \RV^{(m)}_t$,
  where $\E_t$ denotes the conditional expectation given information available at the forecast origin on day $t$,
  and $\RV^{(d)}_t$, $\RV^{(w)}_t$, and $\RV^{(m)}_t$ denote the average daily realized variance over the
  preceding 1, 5, and 22 trading days, respectively. Because all three components represent daily realized
  variances aggregated at the daily, weekly, and monthly horizons, forecasting the realized variance of a
  specific intraday interval lies outside this standard daily specification. Our benchmark carries the HAR
  structure to the intraday interval, and the question we ask is how much a large set of exogenous predictors adds
  to it.\newline

\item \textbf{Economic evaluation of volatility forecasts.} A long tradition values volatility forecasts by the
  profits they earn trading options: a trader buys (sells) straddles when the price implied by the variance forecast
  exceeds (falls short of) the market price, and competing forecasts are ranked by the returns that result. Because
  conventional error measures are only weakly related to the profits a forecast earns, forecasts are judged on both.
  Our economic test brings this evaluation to the intraday horizon, trading forecasts of the closing half hour's
  variance through 0DTE straddles held to the close.\newline
  See \citet{EngleHongKaneNoh1993} and \citet{NohEngleKane1994} on valuing variance forecasts through simulated
  options and S\&P~500 straddle trading, \citet{HarveyWhaley1992} on predictable implied volatility whose trading
  profits do not survive transaction costs, \citet{BandiRussellYang2008} on ranking high-frequency variance
  forecasts by the profits and Sharpe ratios of option trading, and \citet{ChanJhaKalimipalli2009} on statistical
  gains from realized volatility that do not translate into economic gains after costs.

\item \textbf{Shrinkage with many weak signals.} In high-dimensional linear regressions, penalized estimators
  regularize the coefficient vector via
  \[
    \hat{\bm\beta} = \argmin_{\bm\beta} \lVert \bm y - \bm X\bm\beta \rVert_2^2

  penalty weight $\omega_j$ is held constant within each block. Our predictor set is large and its signals
  individually weak, so the comparison of penalized linear models with tree ensembles, and of how their gains
  change with the length of the training window, bears directly on the dense-versus-sparse question.\newline

  \item \textbf{Gradient boosting} \citep{Friedman2001}, implemented via LightGBM \citep{Ke2017} and XGBoost \citep{Chen2016}, minimizes the squared-error loss $\tfrac12 (\tilde y - F)^2$ over boosting rounds $b = 1, \dots, B$ with learning rate $\eta$. Each regression tree $f_b$ partitions the predictor space into $J$ leaves with leaf weights $\bm w$, where leaf $j$ contains the observation subset $\mathcal R_j$ of size $n_j = |\mathcal R_j|$. When the $\ell_1$ leaf penalty $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} = 0$, the additive update and optimal leaf weight take the form
    \begin{align*}
      F_b &= F_{b-1} + \eta f_b, \\
      w_j^\ast &= -\frac{\sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal R_j}\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)}
        {n_j + \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}} .
    \end{align*}
    At round $b$, tree $f_b$ is grown to minimize the regularized second-order objective
    \[
      \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}} \Bigl[\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)
        f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})
        + \tfrac12 f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})^2\Bigr]
      + \gamma^{\mathrm{tree}} J + \lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_1
      + \tfrac12 \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_2^2 ,
    \]
    where $\gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}$ penalizes tree complexity per leaf and $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}}, \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}$ apply $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ shrinkage to the leaf weights $\bm w$.
  \item Every leaf is required to contain at least $n_{\min}$ observations ($n_j \ge n_{\min}$), which corresponds to the minimum leaf size in LightGBM and, under unit Hessian for squared-error loss, the minimum child weight in XGBoost.

\item \textbf{Primary loss criterion.} Our primary statistical loss is the daily quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss of \citet{Patton2011}, which is robust to measurement noise in the realized-variance proxy.
  % 2026-10-16 (user): parked -- Related work no longer surveys forecast evaluation. The cite stays on this loss.

  Because the diurnal factor $s^2_{t,c}$ cancels between $\RV_t = y_t^2 s^2_{t,c}$ (with unwinsorized $y_t$) and $\hat\sigma^2_t = \hat y_t^{\,2} s^2_{t,c}$, the daily loss takes the form
  \[

  \]

  \[
  \overline{\QLIKE} = \bar L = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{oos}}}\sum_{t \in \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}} L_t .
  \]

\item \textbf{Out-of-sample $R^2$.} Following \citet{CampbellThompson2008}, we compute $R^2_{\mathrm{OOS}}$ relative to the expanding historical mean of closing-interval realized variance known at the forecast origin:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Questions.} Which predictors carry the pooled intraday forecasts, and does that change over time? Is the
  exogenous signal dense and weak, spread thinly over many series, or concentrated in a few? Do the series that matter
  do so only on some days, at some bars of the day, or through interactions with other predictors? And how do the
  nonlinear models, the tree ensembles, respond to the non-standard series, the ones outside the HAR benchmark, the
  futures' own realized moments and trading activity, and the VIX?
\item \textbf{What is computed.} The pooled intraday models of the final design (rolling window of
  3{,}000 trading days, 39{,}000 bars; full predictor set of 564 predictors in
  48 groups: each of the 46 exogenous series with its 12 predictors, the HAR
  components and the calendar dummies), explained at monthly origins.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Origins $k = 1, \dots, K$, $K = 126$: one every 21 trading days, at the
    10:00 bar, from 2~January~2014 to 5~April~2024. Origin $k$'s model forecasts its block $\mathcal O_k$,
    the 21 trading days up to the next origin (the last block: 18 days); the blocks
    partition all $|\mathcal O| = 33{,}970$ bars from 2~January~2014 to 30~April~2024. The penalties and the
    tree configurations were chosen on the last pre-sample fold, which ends on 31~December~2013, so no explained bar
    lies in a tuning fold.
  \item Tree ensembles (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest): at each origin the model is refit on the
    39{,}000 bars before it, as its every-bar walk refits at that bar, and held for the block.
    Path-dependent TreeSHAP values \citep{lundberg2020local} of every bar $(t,i) \in \mathcal O_k$, on the scale of
    the forecast, add up to it, and a group's value sums its predictors' values:
    \[
      \hat y_{t,i} = \phi_{k,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
      \phi_{t,i,A} = \sum_{j \in A} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
      s_A = \frac{I_A}{\sum_{B} I_B}, \quad I_A = \frac{1}{|\mathcal O|} \sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal O} |\phi_{t,i,A}| ,
    \]
    with $\phi_{k,0}$ the model's expected forecast over its own training sample (the trees' node covers), so no
    background sample is chosen.
  \item Linear models (ridge, lasso, elastic net): the walk's own coefficients at each origin on the
    window-standardized predictors, which the penalty acts on, $\gamma_{k,j} = \hat\beta_{k,j}\,\mathrm{sd}_{k,j}$,
    and a group's share $S_A = \sum_k \sum_{j \in A} |\gamma_{k,j}| / \sum_k \sum_{j} |\gamma_{k,j}|$; penalties as
    frozen for this window (ridge \ensuremath{10^{3}}, lasso \ensuremath{10^{-4}}, elastic net \ensuremath{10^{-3}}), with the penalty
    factor 0.01 on the HAR components and the calendar dummies.
  \item Two classes, fixed before any SHAP value was computed. Standard (12 groups): the HAR components,
    the calendar dummies, the futures' seven realized moments, the VIX, and the futures' volume and trade count.
    Non-standard: the other 36 series (constituent liquidity, the equal- and value-weighted market
    moments, StockTwits sentiment, volatility demand, the FOMC calendar, VVIX and VIX3M).
  \item Intervals: 95\% moving-block bootstrap over the origins (blocks of 12 origins, about a year;
    2{,}000 resamples), paired across models. They measure the variation over the span's origins, not the
    sampling error of one fit.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Scope.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The trees and the linear models are measured differently (mean absolute SHAP value against $|\gamma|$), so
    the comparison is of rankings and of shares of each model's own measure, not of magnitudes. With the penalty
    factor on the HAR block, the linear models' HAR shares are not comparable with the trees'; comparisons across
    model types use the exogenous total.
  \item A SHAP share measures how much a series moves the forecast, not how much it improves its accuracy.
  \item Between correlated predictors (the equal- and value-weighted versions of a series, a series' value and
    availability averages) the credit follows the trees' split choices; summing over a group removes the split
    within the group, not the split between groups.
  \item SHAP explains each origin's refit held for its block, whereas the walks refit at every bar; the two
    coincide at the origin bars. There the refits equal the walks' forecasts bit for bit at 126,
    126 and 126 of the 126 origins (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest). The
    linear coefficients are the walks' own (their replayed forecasts match to \ensuremath{8.9\times 10^{-16}}).
  \item XGBoost computes SHAP values in single precision: they add up to the forecast within \ensuremath{2.9\times 10^{-6}}
    (tolerance \ensuremath{10^{-5}}); LightGBM's and the forest's within \ensuremath{4.8\times 10^{-14}}.
  \item Not covered yet: the MinGRU network (parked), and the ablations (leave one category out, then one series out
    within the categories that matter), which are not run.
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Relation to intraday option-return prediction.} \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026} also trade
  S\&P~500 index options on half-hourly machine-learning forecasts, but they forecast the delta-hedged return of each
  contract from its characteristics and sort the contracts into decile long--short portfolios every half hour. Their
  portfolio returns are computed at mid-quotes, and they note that trading each option at its quoted bid and ask
  prices would erase a large share of the profits. Our test differs in three respects: the forecast is the variance
  of the underlying over the closing half hour, set against the straddle's implied variance; the position is a
  single at-the-money 0DTE straddle a day, entered at 15:30 and held to expiration; and its Sharpe ratios are
  reported at quoted bid/ask prices as well as at mid-quotes. Because the two designs differ in horizon, position,
  and sample period, their Sharpe ratios are not directly comparable.

\item \textbf{Comparison with machine-learning option portfolios.} Our straddle trades share their market and bar
  length with those of \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026}, who trade S\&P~500 index options on machine-learning
  forecasts of their half-hourly delta-hedged returns. The overlap is one of setting: our trades apply realized
  variance forecasts, whereas their option returns are the object of the forecasts, and the two strategies differ in
  what they trade and in what their Sharpe ratios measure.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Their decile long--short portfolios, re-formed every half hour across the cross-section of contracts over
    eight test months of 2015, reach half-hourly Sharpe ratios of 0.55 and
    0.67 for their two best specifications (31.27 and 38.47 annualized),
    gross and at mid-quotes. Weighting the contracts by open interest lowers them to 0.35 and
    0.56, and by their own account trading each option at its quoted bid and ask would erase a large
    share of the profits.
  \item Our strategy holds one at-the-money straddle a day, signed by the variance forecast of the closing half
    hour. On the full predictor set its annualized Sharpe ratio is 1.67--1.96 at
    mid-quotes and 1.31--1.60 at quoted bid/ask prices over the 614 post-warmup days, against
    \ensuremath{-}0.12 and \ensuremath{-}0.46 for the unconditional short straddle; its gain over that benchmark is
    statistically significant in 1 of the 12 pooled forecasts and is concentrated on a few
    days (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_results}).
  % 2026-10-25 (user, step 1 of the gap analysis): parked -- "ours come from timing the variance premium of the
  % closing half hour with a realized variance forecast": no decomposition of the straddle profits backs it yet, and
  % the short straddle shows no detectable variance risk premium in the sample (Section 7). Was: "Their profits come
  % from ranking contracts on predicted returns, which they trace to mispricing; ours come from timing the variance
  % premium of the closing half hour with a realized variance forecast."
  \item Their profits come from ranking contracts on predicted returns, which they trace to mispricing; ours rest on
    the sign of a realized variance forecast against the implied variance of a single straddle. Their gross Sharpe
    ratios are far larger and rest on a turnover that quoted spreads would largely absorb; ours are modest, but they
    come from a single trade a day and are reported at quoted bid/ask prices.
  \end{itemize}

\subsection{Closing-interval standardization}
\label{sec:rh_close_scale}
The closing-interval model of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} standardizes the averages of series values on its
own window $\mathcal{W}_t$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}). Rows $t'$ are trading days ($i = c$ suppressed):
\[
  z^{(k)}_{t} = \frac{\bar u^{(k)}_{t} - \operatorname{med}_{t' \in \mathcal{W}_t} \bar u^{(k)}_{t'}}
    {\max\bigl\{\mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}_{t},\ 0.01 \max_{t' \le t} \mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}_{t'},\
      \mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t}\bigr\}},
  \qquad \mathrm{IQR}^{(k)}_{t} = \mathrm{IQR}\bigl\{\bar u^{(k)}_{t'} : t' \in \mathcal{W}_t\bigr\}.
\]
\begin{itemize}
\item $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t}$: IQR of $\bar u^{(k)}_{t'}$, $t' < t$, over rows whose $k$-interval averaging
  window is fully observed.
\item Column whose mode accounts for at least 20\% of rows: $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t}$ also excludes rows at
  the mode.
\item $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t} = 1$ until 8 such rows exist.
\item $\bar a^{(k)}$, $\bar\chi^{(k)}$: not standardized. HAR components, calendar dummies:
  $\mathrm{IQR}^{\ast(k)}_{t} = 0$.
\item $t < W$: the first window's statistics.
\end{itemize}

We obtain its quantiles by simulation, computing the same statistic on 1{,}000{,}000 independent series of 1{,}000 i.i.d.\ standard normal draws with bandwidth $1{,}000\,b$.   \begin{itemize}
  \item Each of 4{,}999 bootstrap samples joins blocks of 10 consecutive days, drawn with replacement from the $T$ post-warmup days arranged on a circle; both strategies are resampled on the same days.   \item The $p$-value is two-sided, the share of samples with $|\Delta\SR^{*} - \Delta\SR| \ge |\Delta\SR|$. The block length is fixed rather than calibrated, and the random seed is fixed.

The studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008} tests the equality of the Sharpe ratios of the daily returns pooled over the $T$ days, the ratio of the mean to the standard deviation of all $T$ returns. It is the test of the second alternative definition in Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_sharpe_defs} and is reported beside the bootstrap test above in Table~\ref{tab:rh_app_hac_robust}.

  returns, made volatility observable and forecastable \citep{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003,
  BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}, and the heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) model of \citet{Corsi2009} has become
  the benchmark for forecasting it at the daily horizon. We carry this program to a single intraday interval, the
  closing half hour of the trading day, and ask what predictors from outside the index's own price history add to
  the HAR benchmark there.
\item \textbf{Research question.} We investigate whether incorporating exogenous predictors improves intraday
  % 2026-10-17 (user, new-notes 1): parked -- the target is built from front-month E-mini futures (03_data, Realized moments). Was: "forecasts of the realized variance of the S\&P 500"

  \begin{itemize}
  \item Specifically, at the 15:30 ET forecast origin on trading day $t$, we seek to predict $\RV_t$, which
    denotes the realized variance over the 15:30--16:00 closing interval (see Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}).
  % 2026-10-22 (user): parked -- the pooled models are estimated on the 13 regular-hours bars (E34).     day, and we evaluate its out-of-sample predictions on the forecast issued at 15:30 for the closing half hour.
  \item To isolate the contribution of the additional covariates, we compare the full predictor set against the
    HAR benchmark; the exogenous series constitute the exact difference between the two sets (see
    Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}).

\item \textbf{Motivation for the HAR baseline.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the standard HAR regression models
  realized volatility solely as a linear function of its own past lags. Consequently, it omits a rich set of
  exogenous variables available by 15:30: higher-order realized moments of the futures; the intraday trading of
  the index's constituents, through their realized moments, liquidity, and order-flow imbalance; option-implied
  volatility; the calendar of FOMC announcements; and alternative data, namely social-media sentiment and attention
  from StockTwits and the net option vega bought by non-market-makers (volatility demand). Alternative data of this
  kind have been used to forecast daily realized volatility \citep{AudrinoSigristBallinari2020,CaporinPoli2017}; we
  ask whether they help at the intraday horizon.

\item \textbf{Realized variance and the HAR model.} Following \citet{Corsi2009}, the heterogeneous
  autoregressive (HAR) model specifies the conditional expectation of next-day realized variance as a linear
  function of past realized variances aggregated over daily, weekly, and monthly horizons:
  $\E_t[\RV^{(d)}_{t+1}] = \beta_0 + \beta_d\, \RV^{(d)}_t + \beta_w\, \RV^{(w)}_t + \beta_m\, \RV^{(m)}_t$,
  where $\E_t$ denotes the conditional expectation given information available at the forecast origin on day $t$,
  and $\RV^{(d)}_t$, $\RV^{(w)}_t$, and $\RV^{(m)}_t$ denote the average daily realized variance over the
  preceding 1, 5, and 22 trading days, respectively. Because all three components represent daily realized
  variances aggregated at the daily, weekly, and monthly horizons, forecasting the realized variance of a
  specific intraday interval lies outside this standard daily specification. Our benchmark carries the HAR
  structure to the intraday interval, and the question we ask is how much a large set of exogenous predictors adds
  to it.\newline
  See \citet{Corsi2009}, \citet{AndersenBollerslevDieboldLabys2003}, \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2004},
  \citet{AndersenBollerslevDiebold2007}, \citet{CorsiMittnikPigorschPigorsch2008},
  \citet{BollerslevPattonQuaedvlieg2016}, \citet{BekiermanManner2018}, \citet{BennedsenLundePakkanen2022},
  \citet{HansenHuangShek2012}, and \citet{AndersenBollerslevChristoffersenDiebold2006}.
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- Related work does not describe our estimators. The components, the square-root
  % target, and the 15:30 origin belong in Methods. Was: "... on day $t$ (here 15:30 ET) and ... Our HAR components
  % $\bar y^{(k)}_t$ take the same averages over $k$ intraday intervals of $y$, the square root of realized variance
  % divided by its diurnal adjustment (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data})."
  % \editc{red}{E1}{Related work says the HAR components average $y$... Predictors and Methods average $\tilde y$.}
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-24 (user, framing pass): parked -- the sentence without the link to our pooling. Was: "In a multivariate
  % setting, the panel HAR framework of \citet{BollerslevHoodHussLebedev2018} estimates a single pooled regression
  % jointly across a cross-section of assets."
  \item In a multivariate setting, the panel HAR framework of \citet{BollerslevHoodHussLebedev2018} estimates a
    single pooled regression jointly across a cross-section of assets; our intraday models pool in the same spirit,
    across the intraday intervals of one index rather than across assets.
    % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- this named our estimator. Was: "the cross-asset counterpart of our intraday
    % model, which pools the intraday intervals of one index."
    % Key says "Lebedev"; the bib's author field (correctly) says Pedersen -- \citet prints the author field.
  \item For the theoretical foundations of realized variance, see \citet{BarndorffNielsenShephard2002}.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now a \citet key in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Barndorff-Nielsen--Shephard 2002 (realized variance)}.

\item \textbf{Diurnal pattern.} It is well documented that intraday return volatility exhibits a pronounced
  U-shaped pattern across the trading session. To account for this periodicity, standard practice scales intraday
  realized variance by a diurnal factor estimated from the corresponding clock-time interval on prior trading
  % 2026-10-24 (user): parked -- the framing sentence before it cited the intraday volatility forecasting precedents.
  % Was: "We follow this practice; it is what allows one model to be estimated across all intervals of the trading
  % day."

  % session and delete the overnight return (Engle--Sokalska, Sec. 2.1; Zhang et al., Sec. 3). Was: "days. We follow
  % this practice; it is what allows one model to be estimated across all intervals of the trading day, as in ..."
  days. We follow this practice; it is what allows one model to be estimated across the intervals of the regular
  trading session, as in the intraday volatility forecasts of \citet{EngleSokalska2012}, whose multiplicative
  component GARCH model writes intraday volatility as the product of daily, diurnal, and stochastic intraday
  components and is estimated pooled across a large cross-section of stocks, and, with machine-learning models over
  intraday buckets, of \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}. Both leave the overnight return out of estimation, and
  so do we: our models are estimated on the regular-hours intervals only (Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}).\newline
  % 2026-10-16 (user, E1): parked -- the display was our target, not the literature's. Was:
  % "divides by a diurnal adjustment, here $y_{t,i} = \sqrt{\RV_{t,i}/s^2_{t,i}}$, with $\RV_{t,i}$ the realized
  % variance of intraday interval $i$ on day $t$ and $s^2_{t,i}$ its diurnal adjustment."
  See \citet{AndersenBollerslev1997} on intraday periodicity, \citet{EngleGallo2006} on intraday range and
  volatility measures as indicators of daily volatility, and \citet{HizmeriBevilacqua2025} on morning
  volatility uncertainty.
  % 2026-10-15 (notation pass): EngleGallo2006 is a multiple-indicators model of daily volatility, not a periodicity
  % paper; its claim is narrowed to what it shows.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item See also \citet{TaylorXu1997} on diurnal volatility adjustments and \citet{EngleSokalska2012} on
    multiplicative decompositions of intraday volatility.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Taylor--Xu 1997 (periodicity factor); Engle--Sokalska 2012 (intraday volatility)}.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-25 (user): new bullet -- overnight data enter the predictors, not the estimation sample.
\item \textbf{Overnight information.} Volatility forecasts for the trading session have long used information from
  outside it: after-hours realized variance helps predict next-day stock volatility \citep{ChenYuZivot2012}, and
  overnight information, including the realized volatility of related assets that trade while the home market is
  closed, improves realized volatility forecasts \citep{TodorovaSoucek2014}. For the S\&P 500 futures, which trade
  nearly around the clock, \citet{StroudJohannes2014} model all 5-minute returns, not only those of the regular
  session, and argue that deleting the overnight returns removes important information. These studies forecast
  daily or session volatility. We carry the idea to the intraday interval: our models are estimated and scored on
  the regular-hours intervals, as in the precedents above, while their predictors, the trailing averages of the
  target and of the exogenous series, are computed over the futures' full intraday grid, overnight intervals
  included (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}).
\item \textbf{0DTE options and the variance risk premium.} The variance risk premium, defined as the difference
  between option-implied variance and expected realized variance,
  $\E^{\mathbb{Q}}_t[\RV_t] - \E^{\mathbb{P}}_t[\RV_t]$, under the risk-neutral ($\mathbb Q$) and physical
  ($\mathbb P$) measures (where $\RV_t$ denotes the realized variance through expiration), is empirically
  % 2026-10-24 (user, straddle bullet): parked -- the framing sentence, now split between this bullet (straddle
  % returns, the benchmark) and the new economic-evaluation bullet. Was: "Our economic application sits at the end of
  % a 0DTE option's life: we ask whether more accurate forecasts of the closing half hour's realized variance, set
  % against the option-implied variance, translate into straddle returns."; and the reading list "See
  % \citet{HizmeriBevilacqua2025}, as well as the foundational option-pricing frameworks of \citet{BlackScholes1973}
  % and \citet{Merton1973}."
  positive on average, so that zero-beta at-the-money straddles and delta-hedged index option positions lose
  money on average; the unconditional short straddle is therefore the natural benchmark for a strategy that trades
  straddles on a variance forecast. Our straddles are 0DTE options held through the closing half hour, the last
  interval of their life.\newline
  See \citet{HizmeriBevilacqua2025}, as well as the foundational option-pricing frameworks of
  \citet{BlackScholes1973} and \citet{Merton1973}; on the returns of index straddles and delta-hedged options, see
  \citet{CovalShumway2001}, \citet{BakshiKapadia2003}, and \citet{BroadieChernovJohannes2009}.
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-24 (user, straddle bullet): parked -- the 0DTE reading list before Chong--Todorov and Muravyev--Ni. Was:
  % "On zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options, see \citet{BandiFusariReno2023}, \citet{BeckmeyerBrangerGayda2023},
  % \citet{BrogaardHanWon2023}, \citet{DimErakerVilkov2024}, \citet{Vilkov2026}, and \citet{AlmeidaFreireHizmeri2025};
  % on the variance risk premium more broadly, see \citet{CarrWu2009} and \citet{BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}."

  % that removes its positive net Sharpe ratios, with a revision in progress.
  \item On zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options, see \citet{BandiFusariReno2023},
    \citet{BeckmeyerBrangerGayda2023}, \citet{BrogaardHanWon2023}, \citet{DimErakerVilkov2024},
    \citet{Vilkov2026}, and \citet{AlmeidaFreireHizmeri2025}; on whether equity and 0DTE options markets agree
    about volatility, and on trading their disagreement, see \citet{ChongTodorov2026}; on why option returns differ
    between the trading day and the night, see \citet{MuravyevNi2020}; on the variance risk premium more broadly,
    see \citet{CarrWu2009} and \citet{BollerslevTauchenZhou2009}.
  % 2026-10-15 (bib pass): parked -- the [to add] placeholder, now \citet keys in references.bib. Was:
  % \item \todo{to add: Bandi--Fusari--Ren\`o 2023; Beckmeyer--Branger--Gayda 2023; Brogaard--Han--Won 2023;
  %   Dim--Eraker--Vilkov 2024; Vilkov, 0DTE trading rules; Almeida--Freire--Hizmeri 2025; Carr--Wu 2009;
  %   Bollerslev--Tauchen--Zhou 2009}.

% 2026-10-24 (user): new bullet -- the gap in the literature our economic test fills (option-based evaluation of
% volatility forecasts); references verified against each paper's abstract or text.
\item \textbf{Economic evaluation of volatility forecasts.} A long tradition values volatility forecasts by the
  profits they earn trading options: a trader buys (sells) straddles when the price implied by the variance forecast
  exceeds (falls short of) the market price, and competing forecasts are ranked by the returns that result. Because
  conventional error measures are only weakly related to the profits a forecast earns, forecasts are judged on both.
  Our economic test brings this evaluation to the intraday horizon, trading forecasts of the closing half hour's
  variance through 0DTE straddles held to the close.\newline
  See \citet{EngleHongKaneNoh1993} and \citet{NohEngleKane1994} on valuing variance forecasts through simulated
  options and S\&P~500 straddle trading, \citet{HarveyWhaley1992} on predictable implied volatility whose trading
  profits do not survive transaction costs, \citet{BandiRussellYang2008} on ranking high-frequency variance
  forecasts by the profits and Sharpe ratios of option trading, and \citet{ChanJhaKalimipalli2009} on statistical
  gains from realized volatility that do not translate into economic gains after costs.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item On straddle returns sorted on the gap between realized and implied volatility, see
    \citet{GoyalSaretto2009}; on profits versus conventional error measures, see \citet{LeitchTanner1991} and
    \citet{CenesizogluTimmermann2012}.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Machine learning for volatility and returns.} A growing literature models conditional return and
  volatility dynamics via flexible nonlinear mappings $f(\bm x_t)$ of a high-dimensional predictor vector

  % intervals of the day and predictors built from realized volatility alone; we keep that design for the S\&P~500
  % and ask what a large set of exogenous predictors adds, comparing penalized linear models with tree ensembles."

  % characteristics and sort the contracts into long--short portfolios."
  At the intraday horizon, machine learning has also reached option returns: \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026}
  predict the half-hourly delta-hedged returns of S\&P~500 index options from contract characteristics, Greeks, and
  option-implied measures of the index's return distribution, and sort the contracts into long--short portfolios.
  % 2026-10-25 (user: lineage in the realized volatility literature; option trading as an application): parked --
  % "We forecast the volatility of the index itself, and options enter only through our economic test."
  Our forecasts belong to the realized volatility literature: we forecast the volatility of the index itself, and
  options enter only as an application of these forecasts. The closest machine-learning precedent for our setting,
  \citet{ZhangZhangCucuringuQian2024}, forecasts realized volatility over intraday buckets for a cross-section of
  stocks, fitting one model across all buckets of the day and, in its universal variant, across stocks, with

  hyperparameter optimization, see \citet{Akiba2019} (Optuna).
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- NN content parked for now. Was: "...; realized volatility: \citet{Bucci2020},

\item \textbf{Shrinkage with many weak signals.} In high-dimensional linear regressions, penalized estimators
  regularize the coefficient vector via
  \[
    \hat{\bm\beta} = \argmin_{\bm\beta} \lVert \bm y - \bm X\bm\beta \rVert_2^2
      + \lambda\bigl(\alpha \lVert\bm\beta\rVert_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2} \lVert\bm\beta\rVert_2^2\bigr)
  \]
  for a response vector $\bm y$, a predictor matrix $\bm X$, and an overall penalty strength $\lambda$, nesting
  ridge regression ($\alpha = 0$) and the lasso ($\alpha = 1$) as special cases; multi-penalty ridge extensions
  assign distinct regularization weights across feature blocks via $\lambda \sum_j \omega_j \beta_j^2$, where the
  penalty weight $\omega_j$ is held constant within each block. Our predictor set is large and its signals
  individually weak, so the comparison of penalized linear models with tree ensembles, and of how their gains
  change with the length of the training window, bears directly on the dense-versus-sparse question.\newline

  elastic net, and \citet{vandeWiel2021multipenalty} and \citet{vanWieringen2023ridge} on multi-penalty ridge
  estimation.

\section{Methods}
\label{sec:rh_methods}
\subsection{Problem formulation}
\label{sec:rh_methods_setup}
\begin{itemize}

% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- "re-estimated daily" -> "re-estimated every period" (two training schemes,

Was: "A period corresponds to a 30-minute intraday interval under our pooled intraday scheme (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}) and to a trading day for the daily benchmark forecast (Section~\ref{sec:rh_results_eval})."
% 2026-10-23 (phase 2, final design): the pooled models' every-interval origin added (Table 1 scores every
% regular-hours bar: writeup/make_rehaul_oos_rerun.py; the trailing averages are lagged one interval, Section 4, and
% the final runs refit at every bar, results/pooled_trees_final_2014start_w3000/forecasts.json "refit": "bar"). The
% two sentences before it are unchanged.
\item \textbf{Rolling-window out-of-sample exercise.} We conduct a rolling-window out-of-sample forecasting exercise in which each model is re-estimated every period using only predictors in the information set $\mathcal F_t$ available at the 15:30 ET forecast origin. A period corresponds to a 30-minute intraday interval under our pooled intraday scheme (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}). The 15:30 origin is that of the closing interval $i = c$; the pooled models also forecast every other interval $(t,i)$ of their estimation sample, each at its own origin, the start of the interval, from the information available then (Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos}).
% 2026-10-25 (user): the regular-hours set named; the pooled models are estimated on it (segment rth13 of
% src/backtest/segmentation.py, lag scope "global": trailing averages on the full grid, rows sliced after).
\item \textbf{Notation.} We index trading days by $t = 1, \dots, T$ and the 30-minute intraday intervals of day $t$ (including the overnight session) by $i = 1, \dots, M$, where $i = c$ denotes the closing half-hour interval (15:30--16:00 ET). The regular-hours intervals, those ending 10:00 to 16:00~ET, form the subset $\mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}} \subset \{1, \dots, M\}$, which contains $c$.
  \begin{itemize}
  % 2026-10-16 (formula pass): parked -- RV_{t,i} = sum_k r_{t,i,k}^2 and the lag (t, i-j) are defined once
  % in Data (sec:rh_data). Was: the sum, with r_{t,i,k} the kth one-minute log return and N_{t,i} <= 30
  % (Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold and Labys 2003); and "(t, i-j): the jth retained interval before (t,i)".
  \item Realized variance $\RV_{t,i}$ and the lag operator $(t, i-j)$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}. Our primary forecast target is the realized variance of the closing interval, $\RV_t \equiv \RV_{t,c}$.
  \item We denote by $\mathcal F_t$ the information set containing all data observed through 15:30 ET on day $t$, and write $\E_t[\cdot] \equiv \E[\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_t]$ and $\Var_t(\cdot) \equiv \Var(\,\cdot \mid \mathcal F_t)$ for the corresponding conditional expectation and variance.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- the window lengths 20 and 5 are implementation; they move to Experimental setup
% (sec:rh_exp_samples) as n_d and \underline n_d. Was:
% \mathcal D_{t,i} = \{\text{last } 20 \text{ trading days } t' < t \text{ with interval } i\}, \qquad
% |\mathcal D_{t,i}| \ge 5 . ... \item Intervals with $|\mathcal D_{t,i}| < 5$: not scored.
\item \textbf{Diurnal adjustment.} Following \citet{AndersenBollerslev1997}, we remove the intraday diurnal pattern using the trailing sample mean of realized variance in the same time-of-day interval strictly prior to day $t$:
  \begin{gather*}
    s^2_{t,i} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal D_{t,i}|}\sum_{t' \in \mathcal D_{t,i}} \RV_{t',i}, \\
    \mathcal D_{t,i} = \{\text{last } n_{\mathrm{d}} \text{ trading days } t' < t \text{ with interval } i\}, \qquad
    |\mathcal D_{t,i}| \ge \underline n_{\mathrm{d}} .
  \end{gather*}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item For intervals with $|\mathcal D_{t,i}| < \underline n_{\mathrm{d}}$, we set $s^2_{t,i} = 1$ and exclude the interval from evaluation. The window parameters $n_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $\underline n_{\mathrm{d}}$ are given in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}.
  \end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Regression target.} To stabilize the variance, we take the square root of the diurnally adjusted realized variance and winsorize the resulting series at rolling lower and upper empirical quantiles:

    y_{t,i} = \sqrt{\RV_{t,i} / s^2_{t,i}}, \qquad
    \mathcal Y_{t,i} = \{y_{t,i-j} : j = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{w}}\}, \\
    \tilde y_{t,i} = \clip\bigl(y_{t,i},\; \underline Q_{t,i},\; \overline Q_{t,i}\bigr).

The quantile levels and window length $n_{\mathrm{w}}$ are reported in Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_samples}.

\item \textbf{Back-transformation.} To obtain a variance forecast in raw units, we square the fitted volatility and multiply by the diurnal factor without post-estimation recalibration:

The sentence under the display then calls $\hat y_t$ a forecast of $y_t$. The loss that is scored, QLIKE, is computed from the unwinsorized $\RV_{t,c}$. The number that comes out of the regression is a fitted value for the clipped series. The sentence describes the square of that fitted value as a forecast of the unclipped series.}

\item \textbf{Rolling estimation window.} We let $\mathcal I$ denote the subset of intraday intervals included in estimation. Under the intraday scheme, the estimation window at origin $(t,i)$ is $\mathcal W_{t,i}$ (Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_exp_schemes}), consisting of the $W$ most recent intervals in $\mathcal I$ prior to $(t,i)$ (the intervals in $\mathcal I$ and the value of $W$ are given in Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}).

% gap of $n_{\mathrm{gap}}$ observations, and a validation subsample of $n_{\mathrm{val}}$ observations: [the display

\item \textbf{Hyperparameter-selection splits.} In line with \citet{gu2020empirical}, every split runs forward in time: an estimation subsample, an embargo gap of $n_{\mathrm{gap}}$ observations, and a validation subsample of $n_{\mathrm{val}}$ observations. We use two forms of split.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Pre-sample split.} The pooled linear models of Table~\ref{tab:rh_oos} choose their penalties once, on a split that ends before the first forecast, and hold them fixed for every forecast; the closing-interval linear models choose theirs on pre-sample folds of the same form (Appendix~\ref{app:rh_closing_sample}). The estimation subsample is a full window of $W$ observations, so that each candidate penalty is fitted on as many observations as a forecast. For a split whose validation subsample ends just before $(t,i)$,
  \begin{gather*}
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{est}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - n_{\mathrm{gap}} - W), \dots, (t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - n_{\mathrm{gap}} - 1)\}, \\
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{gap}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - n_{\mathrm{gap}}), \dots,
      (t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}} - 1)\}, \\
    \mathcal W^{\mathrm{val}}_{t,i} = \{(t,\, i - n_{\mathrm{val}}), \dots, (t,\, i - 1)\}.

  \item \textbf{Gradient boosting} \citep{Friedman2001}, implemented via LightGBM \citep{Ke2017} and XGBoost \citep{Chen2016}, minimizes the squared-error loss $\tfrac12 (\tilde y - F)^2$ over boosting rounds $b = 1, \dots, B$ with learning rate $\eta$. Each regression tree $f_b$ partitions the predictor space into $J$ leaves with leaf weights $\bm w$, where leaf $j$ contains the observation subset $\mathcal R_j$ of size $n_j = |\mathcal R_j|$. When the $\ell_1$ leaf penalty $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} = 0$, the additive update and optimal leaf weight take the form
    \begin{align*}
      F_b &= F_{b-1} + \eta f_b, \\
      w_j^\ast &= -\frac{\sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal R_j}\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)}
        {n_j + \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}} .
    \end{align*}
    At round $b$, tree $f_b$ is grown to minimize the regularized second-order objective
    \[
      \sum_{(t',i') \in \mathcal W_{t,i}} \Bigl[\bigl(F_{b-1}(\bm x_{t',i'}) - \tilde y_{t',i'}\bigr)
        f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})
        + \tfrac12 f_b(\bm x_{t',i'})^2\Bigr]
      + \gamma^{\mathrm{tree}} J + \lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_1
      + \tfrac12 \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}} \lVert \bm w \rVert_2^2 ,
    \]
    where $\gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}$ penalizes tree complexity per leaf and $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{tree}}, \lambda_2^{\mathrm{tree}}$ apply $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ shrinkage to the leaf weights $\bm w$.

\subsection{Variable importance}
\label{sec:rh_fi}
\ifdefined\rhfipNOrigins\else\input{generated/rehaul_fip_numbers}\fi
% 2026-10-22 (user): rerun note.
% 2026-10-23 (user, RR): parked -- the pooled variable importance is now computed on the final runs (linear models and
% the three trees, W = 3,000); the preliminary run results/rehaul_fi_pooled13_2026-10-22 (151 re-estimations, earlier
% design) is superseded and not printed. Was:
% "\editc{orange}{RR}{Decision: the pooled linear variable importance is computed on the current design (151 monthly
% re-estimations, results/rehaul\_fi\_pooled13\_2026-10-22: dense across variables, sparse within each) and goes in after
% the rerun of the pooled models; the tree analysis is to be decided.\\Problem: this subsection is still a placeholder.
% See the notes to the authors, ``Rerun pending''.}"
% 2026-10-23 (coordinator, tree learning curve): parked -- the note's "trees at the robustness window" item, now scoped
% to the SHAP values (the trees' accuracy across windows is in, tab:rh_fip_lc). Was: "...; the trees at the
% \rhfipWMax-day robustness window (only the linear models are computed there). The forest's walk gate is complete
% (\rhfipRfGateEq{} of \rhfipNOrigins{} origins).}"
\editc{orange}{RR}{Decision (user, 2026-10-22/23): variable importance on the final pooled runs at the main window, the linear models' standardized coefficients and the tree ensembles' TreeSHAP values at \rhfipNOrigins{} monthly origins; the preliminary pooled run (results/rehaul\_fi\_pooled13\_2026-10-22) is superseded.\\Still to come: the ablations (leave one category out, then one series out within the categories that matter; not run); the MinGRU network (parked, not covered); the trees' SHAP values at the \rhfipWMax-day robustness window (only the linear models' coefficients are computed there). The trees' accuracy across windows is in: \rhlcNArmsDone{} of the \rhlcNArmsAll{} walks at \rhlcWOne--\rhlcWLong{} days (Table~\ref{tab:rh_fip_lc}). The forest's walk gate is complete (\rhfipRfGateEq{} of \rhfipNOrigins{} origins).}
% 2026-10-23 (user, RR): parked -- the placeholder; the results follow. Was: "Variable importance is not yet computed for
% the pooled intraday model; the closing-interval analysis is parked (note E19)."
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Questions.} Which predictors carry the pooled intraday forecasts, and does that change over time? Is the
  exogenous signal dense and weak, spread thinly over many series, or concentrated in a few? Do the series that matter
  do so only on some days, at some bars of the day, or through interactions with other predictors? And how do the
  nonlinear models, the tree ensembles, respond to the non-standard series, the ones outside the HAR benchmark, the
  futures' own realized moments and trading activity, and the VIX?
\item \textbf{What is computed.} The pooled intraday models of the final design (rolling window of
  \rhfipWindowDays{} trading days, \rhfipWindowBars{} bars; full predictor set of \rhfipNCols{} predictors in
  \rhfipNGroups{} groups: each of the \rhfipNExog{} exogenous series with its \rhfipNPerSeries{} predictors, the HAR
  components and the calendar dummies), explained at monthly origins.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Origins $k = 1, \dots, K$, $K = \rhfipNOrigins$: one every \rhfipOriginEvery{} trading days, at the
    \rhfipBarFirst{} bar, from \rhfipFirstOrigin{} to \rhfipLastOrigin. Origin $k$'s model forecasts its block $\mathcal O_k$,
    the \rhfipOriginEvery{} trading days up to the next origin (the last block: \rhfipLastBlock{} days); the blocks
    partition all $|\mathcal O| = \rhfipNRows$ bars from \rhfipFirstOrigin{} to \rhfipLastDay. The penalties and the
    tree configurations were chosen on the last pre-sample fold, which ends on \rhfipTuneLast, so no explained bar
    lies in a tuning fold.
  \item Tree ensembles (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest): at each origin the model is refit on the
    \rhfipWindowBars{} bars before it, as its every-bar walk refits at that bar, and held for the block.
    Path-dependent TreeSHAP values \citep{lundberg2020local} of every bar $(t,i) \in \mathcal O_k$, on the scale of
    the forecast, add up to it, and a group's value sums its predictors' values:
    \[
      \hat y_{t,i} = \phi_{k,0} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
      \phi_{t,i,A} = \sum_{j \in A} \phi_{t,i,j}, \qquad
      s_A = \frac{I_A}{\sum_{B} I_B}, \quad I_A = \frac{1}{|\mathcal O|} \sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal O} |\phi_{t,i,A}| ,
    \]
    with $\phi_{k,0}$ the model's expected forecast over its own training sample (the trees' node covers), so no
    background sample is chosen.
  \item Linear models (ridge, lasso, elastic net): the walk's own coefficients at each origin on the
    window-standardized predictors, which the penalty acts on, $\gamma_{k,j} = \hat\beta_{k,j}\,\mathrm{sd}_{k,j}$,
    and a group's share $S_A = \sum_k \sum_{j \in A} |\gamma_{k,j}| / \sum_k \sum_{j} |\gamma_{k,j}|$; penalties as
    frozen for this window (ridge \rhfipRidgePen, lasso \rhfipLassoPen, elastic net \rhfipEnetPen), with the penalty
    factor \rhfipHarPf{} on the HAR components and the calendar dummies.
  \item Two classes, fixed before any SHAP value was computed. Standard (\rhfipNStd{} groups): the HAR components,
    the calendar dummies, the futures' \rhfipNMom{} realized moments, the VIX, and the futures' volume and trade count.
    Non-standard: the other \rhfipNNonStd{} series (constituent liquidity, the equal- and value-weighted market
    moments, StockTwits sentiment, volatility demand, the FOMC calendar, VVIX and VIX3M).
  \item Intervals: \rhfipCiLevel\% moving-block bootstrap over the origins (blocks of \rhfipBootBlock{} origins, about a year;
    \rhfipBootB{} resamples), paired across models. They measure the variation over the span's origins, not the
    sampling error of one fit.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Scope.}
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The trees and the linear models are measured differently (mean absolute SHAP value against $|\gamma|$), so
    the comparison is of rankings and of shares of each model's own measure, not of magnitudes. With the penalty
    factor on the HAR block, the linear models' HAR shares are not comparable with the trees'; comparisons across
    model types use the exogenous total.
  \item A SHAP share measures how much a series moves the forecast, not how much it improves its accuracy.
  \item Between correlated predictors (the equal- and value-weighted versions of a series, a series' value and
    availability averages) the credit follows the trees' split choices; summing over a group removes the split
    within the group, not the split between groups.
  \item SHAP explains each origin's refit held for its block, whereas the walks refit at every bar; the two
    coincide at the origin bars. There the refits equal the walks' forecasts bit for bit at \rhfipLgbmGateEq,
    \rhfipXgbGateEq{} and \rhfipRfGateEq{} of the \rhfipNOrigins{} origins (LightGBM, XGBoost, random forest). The
    linear coefficients are the walks' own (their replayed forecasts match to \rhfipLinGateMax).
  \item XGBoost computes SHAP values in single precision: they add up to the forecast within \rhfipXgbAddMax{}
    (tolerance \rhfipXgbAddTol); LightGBM's and the forest's within \rhfipAddMaxDouble.
  \item Not covered yet: the MinGRU network (parked), and the ablations (leave one category out, then one series out
    within the categories that matter), which are not run.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Which series matter} (Table~\ref{tab:rh_fip_shares}, Figure~\ref{fig:rh_fip_rank}).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item In the trees the HAR components carry \rhfipHarMin--\rhfipHarMax\% of the total attribution and the
    futures' realized moments \rhfipMomMin--\rhfipMomMax\%. The two leading exogenous series are the same in all
    three, \rhfipTreeTopOne{} and \rhfipTreeTopTwo; \rhfipTreeTopOne{} alone holds \rhfipLgbmTopOneEx,
    \rhfipXgbTopOneEx{} and \rhfipRfTopOneEx\% of the exogenous total.
  \item The non-standard series hold \rhfipLgbmNs\% [\rhfipLgbmNsLo, \rhfipLgbmNsHi], \rhfipXgbNs\%
    [\rhfipXgbNsLo, \rhfipXgbNsHi] and \rhfipRfNs\% [\rhfipRfNsLo, \rhfipRfNsHi] of the total (LightGBM, XGBoost,
    random forest), \rhfipNsExMin--\rhfipNsExMax\% of the exogenous total. Their weight sits in a few series; the five
    largest by the mean over the three trees are \rhfipNsOne{} (\rhfipNsOneMin--\rhfipNsOneMax\% of the total), \rhfipNsTwo{}
    (\rhfipNsTwoMin--\rhfipNsTwoMax\%), \rhfipNsThree{} (\rhfipNsThreeMin--\rhfipNsThreeMax\%), \rhfipNsFour{}
    (\rhfipNsFourMin--\rhfipNsFourMax\%) and \rhfipNsFive{} (\rhfipNsFiveMin--\rhfipNsFiveMax\%). The rest carry
    little: the StockTwits series together \rhfipSentMin--\rhfipSentMax\%, the volatility-demand series together
    \rhfipVdMin--\rhfipVdMax\%, VVIX \rhfipVvixMin--\rhfipVvixMax\%, VIX3M \rhfipVixThreeMMin--\rhfipVixThreeMMax\%.
  % 2026-10-26 (user: "make this explicit"): added -- the late-starting series in the years their value averages
  % are live (writeup/make_rehaul_fi_live.py: \rhfil..., Figure fig:rh_fi_live; yearly shares of the TreeSHAP study).
  \item The pooled shares understate the late-starting series (Figure~\ref{fig:rh_fi_live}). Under the late-start
    rule (Section~\ref{sec:rh_predictors}) their value averages stay at the neutral zero until a full window
    postdates their first print, so for most of the span the trees can use only their availability averages, which
    record when a series prints, not what it prints. Over the full calendar years in which the value averages are
    live, the yearly shares rise: StockTwits from \rhfilStwPreMin--\rhfilStwPreMax\% of the total
    (\rhfilStwPreYears) to \rhfilStwLiveMin--\rhfilStwLiveMax\% (\rhfilStwLiveYears), VIX3M from
    \rhfilVixThreePreMin--\rhfilVixThreePreMax\% to \rhfilVixThreeLiveMin--\rhfilVixThreeLiveMax\%, and volatility
    demand from \rhfilVdPreMin--\rhfilVdPreMax\% to \rhfilVdLiveMin--\rhfilVdLiveMax\% in \rhfilVdLiveYears, its only
    full live year before its feed stops. The VIX's share does not rise (\rhfilVixPreMin--\rhfilVixPreMax\% in
    \rhfilVixPreYears, \rhfilVixLiveMin--\rhfilVixLiveMax\% in \rhfilVixLiveYears), and VVIX is live only from
    \rhfilVvixLiveFrom. Even in the live years the models have seen these values on a small part of their training
    window: at the last origin, \rhfilLastOrigin, the \rhfilWinDays-day window holds live values on
    \rhfilStwWinPct\% of its days for StockTwits, \rhfilVixThreeWinPct\% for VIX3M and \rhfilVdWinPct\% for
    volatility demand (\rhfilVixWinPct\% for the VIX). The live-year shares are the fairer measure of how much the
    trees use the alternative data; like every SHAP share here, they measure use, not a gain in accuracy.
  \item The ridge ranks the series differently. Its largest exogenous series is \rhfipRidgeTopOne{}
    (\rhfipRidgeTopOneEx\% of its exogenous total), and it puts the FOMC calendar near the top: \rhfipFomcUntil{} at
    rank \rhfipRidgeRankFomcUntil{} and \rhfipFomcDay{} at rank \rhfipRidgeRankFomcDay{} of \rhfipNExog, where the
    trees rank them \rhfipTreeRankFomcUntilMin--\rhfipTreeRankFomcUntilMax{} and
    \rhfipTreeRankFomcDayMin--\rhfipTreeRankFomcDayMax. Spearman rank correlation of the \rhfipNExog{} shares with the
    ridge's: \rhfipLgbmSpRidge, \rhfipXgbSpRidge, \rhfipRfSpRidge{} (the two top-\rhfipTopN{} lists share
    \rhfipLgbmTopRidge, \rhfipXgbTopRidge{} and \rhfipRfTopRidge{} series); among the trees: \rhfipSpLgbmXgb{} (LightGBM, XGBoost),
    \rhfipSpLgbmRf{} and \rhfipSpXgbRf{} (each against the forest).
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Dense and weak, or concentrated?}

\section{Economic value of the forecasts}
\label{sec:rh_econ}
% 2026-10-25 (user: the option trades as an application of the realized variance forecasts): added -- the lead.
Our forecasts target the realized variance of the closing half hour, and that target has a direct counterpart in
the options market: a same-day-expiring straddle bought at the start of the closing half hour and held to the close
pays off on the variance realized over that half hour, against the variance implied by its price. We therefore value
the forecasts as the literature on the economic evaluation of volatility forecasts does
(Section~\ref{sec:rh_related}), by the returns of the straddle trades they signal; the main strategy uses each
forecast only through the sign of its difference from the implied variance.
% 2026-10-22 (user): rerun note.
% 2026-10-23 (user, final rerun): parked -- the note before the window choice; the window is decided and the generators read the final rerun (writeup/final_run.py). The closing-interval models of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} are not rerun. See the notes to the authors, ``Rerun pending''.}"
% 2026-10-23 (user, final rerun, phase 2): parked -- note RR resolved: the pooled forecasts of this section are the final rerun, and the interval-shift test and the compounded wealth now run on them (notes E26, E27, N15b resolved below). The closing-interval models of Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} are not rerun.\\Pending (2026-10-23): the statistics over the model set (the interval-shift test and the compounded wealth, notes E26, E27, N15b, N18) are not on the final rerun; the sentences whose wording depends on the final values are rechecked in the second pass.}"

\subsection{The straddle strategy}
\label{sec:rh_econ_strategy}
\begin{itemize}
% 2026-10-22 (user): moved here from the data section (03_data.tex, "Estimation and evaluation samples"): the
% option-trading subsample and the held-out expirations.
\item \textbf{Option-trading sample.} We evaluate the strategy on the option-trading subsample
  $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}), the trading days with a
  same-day SPXW expiration:
  \[
    T_{\mathrm{opt}} = \cmNdays \text{ trading days} = \rhdmExpirationsOos \text{ SPXW expirations}
      - \rhdmEarlyCloses \text{ early-close days}.
  \]
  The \rhdmHeldOutExpirations{} subsequent SPXW expiration dates (\rhdmHeldOut{} full trading days) are held out from
  the present analysis.
% 2026-10-17 (user, E18): parked -- S_t named as the chain's 15:30 underlying print. Was: With the index at $S_t$ at the 15:30 ET forecast origin, ...
\item \textbf{Position.} We trade same-day-expiring (0DTE) SPXW options. With $S_t$ denoting the underlying print on the option chain at the 15:30 ET forecast origin, we select the call and put at the nearest adjacent strikes with live quotes:
  \[
  K_C = \min\{K \ge S_t\}, \qquad K_P = \max\{K \le S_t\}.

\item \textbf{Comparison with machine-learning option portfolios.} Our straddle trades share their market and bar
  length with those of \citet{MaischZhangUlrichZimmer2026}, who trade S\&P~500 index options on machine-learning
  forecasts of their half-hourly delta-hedged returns. The overlap is one of setting: our trades apply realized
  variance forecasts, whereas their option returns are the object of the forecasts, and the two strategies differ in
  what they trade and in what their Sharpe ratios measure.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Their decile long--short portfolios, re-formed every half hour across the cross-section of contracts over
    \extMaischTestMonths{} test months of \extMaischYear, reach half-hourly Sharpe ratios of \extMaischSrGbrt{} and
    \extMaischSrEns{} for their two best specifications (\extMaischSrGbrtAnn{} and \extMaischSrEnsAnn{} annualized),
    gross and at mid-quotes. Weighting the contracts by open interest lowers them to \extMaischSrGbrtOi{} and
    \extMaischSrEnsOi, and by their own account trading each option at its quoted bid and ask would erase a large
    share of the profits.
  \item Our strategy holds one at-the-money straddle a day, signed by the variance forecast of the closing half
    hour. On the full predictor set its annualized Sharpe ratio is \rhrPoolShFullMin--\rhrPoolShFullMax{} at
    mid-quotes and \rhrPoolShXFullMin--\rhrPoolShXFullMax{} at quoted bid/ask prices over the \rheSzDays{} post-warmup days, against
    \rheShortSh{} and \rheShortShX{} for the unconditional short straddle; its gain over that benchmark is
    statistically significant in \rhrPoolShortSig{} of the \rhrPoolN{} pooled forecasts and is concentrated on a few
    days (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_results}).
  % 2026-10-25 (user, step 1 of the gap analysis): parked -- "ours come from timing the variance premium of the
  % closing half hour with a realized variance forecast": no decomposition of the straddle profits backs it yet, and
  % the short straddle shows no detectable variance risk premium in the sample (Section 7). Was: "Their profits come
  % from ranking contracts on predicted returns, which they trace to mispricing; ours come from timing the variance
  % premium of the closing half hour with a realized variance forecast."
  \item Their profits come from ranking contracts on predicted returns, which they trace to mispricing; ours rest on
    the sign of a realized variance forecast against the implied variance of a single straddle. Their gross Sharpe
    ratios are far larger and rest on a turnover that quoted spreads would largely absorb; ours are modest, but they
    come from a single trade a day and are reported at quoted bid/ask prices.
  \end{itemize}

\section{Statistical tests}
\label{sec:rh_methods_tests}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Diebold--Mariano test.} To compare the predictive accuracy of two competing forecasts $A$ and $B$, we apply the \citet{DieboldMariano1995} test to the daily QLIKE loss differentials, incorporating the small-sample adjustment of \citet{HarveyLeybourneNewbold1997} for one-step-ahead forecasts:
  \[
    d_t = L_t^{A} - L_t^{B}, \qquad
    \DM = \sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal O| - 1}{|\mathcal O|}}\;
      \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / |\mathcal O|}} .
  \]
  % 2026-10-15 (finish): parked -- the horizon symbol h (also the boosting Hessian h_{t'}) dropped; every forecast
  % is one step ahead, so h = 1 is substituted: (|O| + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/|O|)/|O| = (|O| - 1)/|O|. Was:
  % \DM = \sqrt{\frac{|\mathcal O| + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/|\mathcal O|}{|\mathcal O|}}\;
  %   \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / |\mathcal O|}}, \qquad h = 1 .
  % 2026-10-15 (notation pass): parked -- the uncorrected and corrected statistics merged into one symbol, \DM
  % (the HLN-corrected one, as the code reports); n scored days -> |O|. Old display:
  % \mathrm{DM} = \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega / n}}, \qquad
  % \mathrm{DM}^{\ast} = \mathrm{DM} \sqrt{\frac{n + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/n}{n}}, \qquad h = 1 .
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Here $A$ and $B$ denote competing forecast series $f_{m,\mathcal X,\mathcal I}$, indexed by the model class $m$, the predictor set $\mathcal X \in \{\mathrm{HAR}, \mathrm{Full}\}$, and the estimation interval set $\mathcal I \in \{\{c\}, \mathcal I_{\mathrm{rh}}\}$.
  % 2026-10-25 (user): parked -- the label \{1, \dots, M\} for the pooled models' set; they are estimated on I_rh.
  % 2026-10-15 (user): parked -- "out-of-sample days"; the evaluation set and the option-data subsample. Was:
  % "\item $\mathcal O$: the out-of-sample days of the exercise, numbered $t = 1, \dots, |\mathcal O|$ in time order;
  %   $\mathcal O = \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, $|\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}| = T_{\mathrm{oos}}$, in the headline
  %   comparison."
  \item The evaluation set $\mathcal O$, indexed chronologically by $t = 1, \dots, |\mathcal O|$, equals the full evaluation span $\mathcal O = \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ ($|\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}| = T_{\mathrm{oos}}$) for statistical accuracy comparisons and the option-data subsample $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}} \subset \mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ for straddle return comparisons (Section~\ref{sec:rh_data}).
  \item We denote by $\bar d$ the sample mean of $d_t$ over $\mathcal O$ and compute two-sided $p$-values under the standard normal distribution as $p = 2\bigl\{1 - \Phi(|\DM|)\bigr\}$.
  \item Under this sign convention, $\DM < 0$ indicates that forecast $A$ achieves a lower average loss than forecast $B$. Throughout the paper, ``statistically significant'' refers to significance at the 5\% level ($p < 0.05$).
  % 2026-10-15 (user): merged from Forecast evaluation (moved from 06_results.tex): the p-value formula, the sign
  % convention and the meaning of "significant". Was: "\item $\bar d$: mean loss differential over $\mathcal O$;
  % two-sided $p$-value from the standard normal."
  % 2026-10-15 (finish): parked -- h dropped (one-step-ahead forecasts). Was:
  % \item $\bar d$: mean loss differential over $\mathcal O$; $h$: forecast horizon; two-sided $p$-value from the
  %   standard normal.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-15 (consolidation): parked -- lag truncation q -> q_NW (q_t is the position), autocovariance lag k -> j (k

% divisor of hat gamma_j is unchanged (FLAG (4) below awaits the user). Old bullets:

\item \textbf{Newey--West long-run variance.} Following \citet{NeweyWest1987}, we estimate the long-run variance $\hat\Omega$ using Bartlett kernel weights with lag truncation parameter $q_{\mathrm{NW}}$:

    \qquad
    \hat\gamma_j = \frac{1}{|\mathcal O|} \sum_{t=j+1}^{|\mathcal O|} (d_t - \bar d)(d_{t-j} - \bar d).
  \]

  \begin{itemize}
  \item For the Diebold--Mariano test, we set the bandwidth according to the plug-in rule $q_{\mathrm{NW}} = \lfloor 4 (|\mathcal O|/100)^{2/9} \rfloor$ (its numerical value on $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{oos}}$ is reported in Section~\ref{sec:rh_exp_setup}).

  % src/evaluation/diebold_mariano.py:33-93.

  % i.e. divides by |O| - k, not |O|; newey_west_t (the return test below) divides by |O|, as displayed.

  % 2026-10-18 (user, E13): FLAG (4) resolved -- dm_test now divides gamma_j by |O| (src/evaluation/diebold_mariano.py:67-68), matching this display.
% 2026-10-15 (consolidation): FLAG (7) resolved -- newey_west_t is also applied to a single strategy's mean return

  % 2026-10-15 (finish): parked -- same content; the formula moved to a display (the inline version left an underfull
  % line). Was:
  % \item \textbf{HAC $t$-statistic of a mean daily return} (Newey--West, no HLN correction):
  %   $t = \bar r / \sqrt{\hat\Omega_r / |\mathcal O|}$, with $\hat\Omega_r$ the Newey--West variance above computed on a
  %   daily return series $r_t$ in place of $d_t$: a single strategy's return (a test of its mean return) or the difference
  %   between two strategies' returns (a test of the mean return differential);

  % notebooks/atm_straddle_lib.py:1240-1261 (newey_west_t).
\item \textbf{Test of a mean daily return.} For any daily return series $r_t$---either the return of an individual trading strategy or the return differential $\Delta_t$ between two strategies---observed on the $T = \rheSzDays$ post-warmup days $\mathcal T_{\mathrm{opt}}^{+}$ (Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}), we test whether its mean is zero with the procedure that \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} recommend for the Newey--West estimator:
  \[
    t = \frac{\bar r}{\sqrt{\hat\Omega_r / T}},
    \qquad
    \hat\Omega_r = \sum_{|j| < S} \Bigl(1 - \frac{|j|}{S}\Bigr) \hat\gamma_j,
    \qquad
    \hat\gamma_j = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=|j|+1}^{T} (r_t - \bar r)(r_{t-|j|} - \bar r),
  \]
  with the Bartlett kernel, bandwidth $S = \lceil 1.3\, T^{1/2} \rceil = \rheHACS$, and fixed-$b$ critical values for $b = S/T$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item The autocovariances divide by $T$, with no small-sample factor; at lag truncation $S - 1$ the estimator equals the Newey--West variance of the previous item.
  \item This bandwidth is larger than that of conventional rules such as $0.75\, T^{1/3}$, which \citet{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018} obtain from the formula of \citet{Andrews1991} for a first-order autoregression with coefficient $0.25$. Combined with fixed-$b$ critical values, it reduces the size distortion of the test when the returns are serially correlated \citep{LazarusLewisStockWatson2018}.
  \item Under the null hypothesis and fixed $b$, the limiting distribution of $t$ is a functional of Brownian motion that depends only on the kernel and on $b$ \citep{KieferVogelsang2005}. We obtain its quantiles by simulation, computing the same statistic on 1{,}000{,}000 independent series of 1{,}000 i.i.d.\ standard normal draws with bandwidth $1{,}000\,b$. This gives the two-sided 5\% critical value \rheHACCV{} and the $p$-values reported in the text, in place of the standard normal value 1.96.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-22 (user, D6): parked -- the Ledoit--Wolf test as the test of every Sharpe statement; it tests the ratio of the pooled daily returns, while the paper's $\SR$ (note D6) averages calendar years, each annualized by its own $A_y$. The Ledoit--Wolf item below is kept as a robustness check. Was: "\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios.} A test of $\bar\Delta = 0$ concerns the mean return differential, not the difference between two Sharpe ratios, which divides each strategy's mean return by its own standard deviation. For every statement about a Sharpe ratio difference we therefore use the studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008}."
\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios.} A test of $\bar\Delta = 0$ concerns the mean return differential, not the difference between two Sharpe ratios, which divides each strategy's mean return by its own standard deviation. For every statement about a Sharpe ratio difference $\Delta\SR = \SR(r^A) - \SR(r^B)$, with $\SR$ the ratio of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}, we therefore use a paired circular block bootstrap of $\Delta\SR$.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Each of \rheBootN{} bootstrap samples joins blocks of \rheBootBlock{} consecutive days, drawn with replacement from the $T$ post-warmup days arranged on a circle; both strategies are resampled on the same days. Each drawn day keeps its own calendar year, and $A_y$ stays at its value in the original sample, so each sample gives $\Delta\SR^{*}$ computed exactly as $\Delta\SR$.
  \item The $p$-value is two-sided, the share of samples with $|\Delta\SR^{*} - \Delta\SR| \ge |\Delta\SR|$. The block length is fixed rather than calibrated, and the random seed is fixed.
  \item The bootstrap is not studentized: $\SR$ averages ratios over calendar years, and no closed-form standard error of that average is used.
  \end{itemize}
\item \textbf{Test of equal Sharpe ratios of the pooled daily returns} (robustness). The studentized circular block bootstrap test of \citet{LedoitWolf2008} tests the equality of the Sharpe ratios of the daily returns pooled over the $T$ days, the ratio of the mean to the standard deviation of all $T$ returns. It is the test of the second alternative definition in Table~\ref{tab:rh_econ_sharpe_defs} and is reported beside the bootstrap test above in Table~\ref{tab:rh_app_hac_robust}.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item With $u = \bigl(\mu_A, \mu_B, \mathrm E[(r^A_t)^2], \mathrm E[(r^B_t)^2]\bigr)$, the difference of the Sharpe ratios of the daily returns, $\mu_A/\sigma_A - \mu_B/\sigma_B$, is a smooth function $f(u)$; its standard error follows from the delta method and the long-run covariance matrix $\Psi$ of $\bigl(r^A_t, r^B_t, (r^A_t)^2, (r^B_t)^2\bigr)$.
  \item The test statistic is $d = |f(\hat u)| / \mathrm{se}(\hat u)$. Each of \rheLWBoot{} bootstrap samples joins blocks of \rheLWBlock{} consecutive days, drawn with replacement from the $T$ post-warmup days arranged on a circle, and gives $d^{*} = |f(\hat u^{*}) - f(\hat u)| / \mathrm{se}(\hat u^{*})$, with $\Psi$ estimated in that sample by the block-based estimator of \citet{LedoitWolf2008}. The $p$-value is $\bigl(\#\{d^{*} \ge d\} + 1\bigr)/(\rheLWBoot + 1)$.
  \item In the original sample, $\Psi$ is estimated with the Bartlett kernel at bandwidth equal to the block length, whose expectation is approximately that of the block-based estimator; \citet{LedoitWolf2008} use a prewhitened quadratic-spectral kernel at this step. The block length is fixed at \rheLWBlock{} days rather than calibrated; the next item reports the number of rejections at block lengths \rheLWBlockLo{} and \rheLWBlockHi{}. The random seed is fixed.
  \item The test concerns the Sharpe ratios of daily returns over the $T$ post-warmup days, without the year-by-year annualization of Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ_measures}.
  \end{itemize}
% 2026-10-22 (user, D6): parked -- the Ledoit--Wolf test as the test of the text's Sharpe statements; now the bootstrap of $\Delta\SR$, with the Ledoit--Wolf $p$ beside it. Was: "... the fixed-$b$ test above; and the $p$-value of the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test. Statements in the text about mean returns use the fixed-$b$ test, and statements about Sharpe ratios use the \citet{LedoitWolf2008} test." and "\item Of the \rhrRobNPairs{} tests of equal Sharpe ratios, \rhrRobLWSig{} reject at the 5\% level with block length \rheLWBlock{}, \rhrRobLWSigLo{} with block length \rheLWBlockLo{} and \rhrRobLWSigHi{} with block length \rheLWBlockHi{}."
\item \textbf{Robustness to the long-run variance estimator.} Table~\ref{tab:rh_app_hac_robust} lists every comparison of strategy returns whose statistical significance Section~\ref{sec:rh_econ} or Appendix~\ref{sec:rh_econ_last30} states.
